sentences.text: In lesson eight, we learned what to do when you hear a fog signal.
Today, we learn what those signals are, and what you sound yourself.
Rule thirty-five applies in or near an area of restricted visibility, by day or by night.
Underway, every signal is repeated at intervals of not more than two minutes.
A power-driven vessel making way sounds one prolonged blast.
That’s you, running slowly home in the fog: one long blast, every two minutes.
A power-driven vessel underway but stopped, not making way, sounds two prolonged blasts, with about two seconds between them.
Then comes one signal shared by a whole group: one prolonged blast followed by two short.
It’s sounded by a vessel not under command, restricted in her ability to maneuver, constrained by her draft, sailing, engaged in fishing, or towing or pushing.
It’s almost everybody above you on the ladder.
So one long and two short means: I’m hampered, stay clear.
And a vessel being towed, or the last vessel of the tow, if she’s manned, sounds one prolonged and three short, right after the tug’s signal if practicable.
A composite pushing unit simply sounds the signals of a power-driven vessel.
